L287: ### 2.3 Lax transformation is fractional-linear
L288: 
L289: Given a non-zero vector $P_{i}$, the $i$th vertex of a polygon ${\mathbf{P}}$, the vectors $Q$ with $[P_{i},Q]=c$ comprise a line $L_{P_{i}}$ parallel to $P_{i}$. Identify $L_{P_{i}}$ with ${\mathbb{R}}$ by parameterizing it as
L290: 
L291:  | $$\frac{cP_{i+1}}{[P_{i},P_{i+1}]}+tP_{i},\ t\in{\mathbb{R}}.$$  |
L292: Let ${\bf P}=(P_{1},\ldots,P_{n})$ be a closed $n$-gon. As described in Introduction, choose a test vector $Q_{1}$ with $[P_{1},Q_{1}]=c$, and consecutively construct vectors $Q_{2},\ldots,Q_{n},Q_{n+1}$ according to (cite42†2 ). We use the notation
L293: 
L294:  | $${\mathcal{L}}_{P_{1}P_{2},c}(Q_{1})=Q_{2},\ {\mathcal{L}}_{P_{2}P_{3},c}(Q_{2})=Q_{3},\ldots$$  |
L295: (we omit $c$ from the notation when it does not lead to confusion). The Lax transformation ${\mathcal{L}}_{{\bf P},c}:L_{P_{1}}\to L_{P_{1}}$ is the composition of these maps. Then ${\bf P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\sim}}{\bf Q}$ if and only if $Q_{1}$ is a fixed point of ${\mathcal{L}}_{{\bf P},c}:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}$.
L296: Likewise, if ${\mathbf{P}}$ is a twisted $n$-gon with monodromy ${\mathcal{M}}_{\bf P}$, then ${\mathcal{M}}_{\bf P}$ sends $L_{P_{1}}$ to $L_{P_{n+1}}$ and, as a map ${\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}$, it is the identity. Hence it is still true that the fixed points of ${\mathcal{L}}_{{\bf P},c}$ give rise to twisted polygons ${\mathbf{Q}}$ such that ${\bf P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\sim}}{\bf Q}$.
L297: ###### Lemma 2.6.
L298: 
L299: The Lax transformations are fractional-linear.
L300: ###### Proof.
L301: 
L302: Denote by $R_{Q_{1},P_{2}}$ the centroaffine reflection that interchanges $Q_{1}$ and $P_{2}$. This map is given by the formula
L303: 
L304:  | $$R_{Q_{1},P_{2}}(X)=\frac{[Q_{1},X]Q_{1}+[X,P_{2}]P_{2}}{[Q_{1},P_{2}]},$$  |  | (9)
L305: 
L306: and one has $Q_{2}=R_{Q_{1},P_{2}}(P_{1})$, that is, ${\mathcal{L}}_{P_{1}P_{2}}(Q_{1})=R_{Q_{1},P_{2}}(P_{1})$.
L307: 
L308: Using the identifications of $L_{P_{1}}$ and $L_{P_{2}}$ with ${\mathbb{R}}$, the map ${\mathcal{L}}_{P_{1}P_{2}}:Q_{1}\mapsto Q_{2}$ becomes
L309:  | $$t\mapsto-\frac{c[P_{1},P_{3}]}{[P_{1},P_{2}][P_{2},P_{3}]}+\frac{[P_{1},P_{2}]^{2}-c^{2}}{t[P_{1},P_{2}]^{2}}=-\frac{cv_{4}}{s_{3}s_{5}}+\frac{s_{3}^{2}-c^{2}}{ts_{3}^{2}},$$  |
L310: 
L311: a fractional-linear transformation. Hence ${\mathcal{L}}_{{\bf P},c}$ is fractional-linear as well. ∎
L312: 
L313: The above fractional-linear transformation is represented by the matrix
L314: 
L315:  | $$\begin{pmatrix}-\dfrac{cv_{4}}{s_{3}s_{5}}&\displaystyle{1-\frac{c^{2}}{s_{3}^{2}}}\\
L316: 1&0\end{pmatrix},$$  |  | (10)
L317: its determinant equals $\displaystyle{\frac{c^{2}}{s_{3}^{2}}-1}$.
L318: 
L319: If the ground field is ${\mathbb{C}}$, a fractional-linear transformation has two fixed points, perhaps, coinciding (unless it is the identity). Over the reals, this number is 0, or 1, 2, or $\infty$.
L320: Over ${\mathbb{C}}$, Lemma cite62†2.6 makes it possible to consider $c$-relation as a map (defined in a Zariski open set of polygons): start with ${\mathbf{P}}$ and choose one of the two $c$-related polygons, say ${\mathbf{Q}}_{1}$. This polygon also has two $c$-related ones, one of which is $-{\mathbf{P}}$, the polygon that is centrally symmetric to ${\mathbf{P}}$. Choose the other polygon $c$-related to ${\mathbf{Q}}_{1}$ and continue in a similar way.
L321: If at the beginning we choose ${\mathbf{Q}}_{2}$ instead of ${\mathbf{Q}}_{1}$ then $-{\mathbf{Q}}_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\sim}}{\mathbf{P}}$, that is, up to central symmetry, we obtain the inverse of the same map.
L322: Over ${\mathbb{R}}$, a polygon may have no $c$-related ones. To have a map, one needs to assume that a $c$-related polygon exists. We shall see in Section cite15†3.1 that the $c$-related polygons have conjugated Lax transformations. This makes it possible to continue in the same way as in the complex case.
L323: ### 2.4 Centroaffine butterflies
L324: 
L325: We show that centroaffine butterflies have trivial Lax transformations for all $c$ (see Figure cite63†5 ) and classify all such quadrilaterals.
L326: 
L327: Figure 5: Two centroaffine butterflies are $c$-related.
L328: ###### Lemma 2.7.
L329: 
L330: The Lax transformation for a quadrilateral is the identity for every $c$ if and only if the quadrilateral is a centroaffine butterfly, or it is obtained from a centroaffine butterfly by reflecting one of the vertices in the origin (an “anti-butterfly”), or its two opposite vertices are symmetric with respect to the origin.
L331: ###### Proof.
L332: 
L333: Assume first that two opposite vertices of a quadrilateral ${\mathbf{P}}$ are not collinear. Applying a linear transformation, assume that
L334: 
L335:  | $$P_{1}=(1,0),\ P_{2}=(a,b),\ P_{3}=(0,1),\ P_{4}=(u,v),\ Q_{1}=(x,y),$$  |
L336: 
L337: so $y=c$. Applying equation (cite64†9 ) twice, we find
L338: 
L339:  | $$Q_{2}=\frac{1}{bx-ay}(ab-xy,b^{2}-y^{2}),\ Q_{3}=\left(-y,\frac{-y\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)+abx+y^{3}}{ab-xy}\right).$$  |
L340: 
L341: Going in the opposite direction, that is, replacing $(a,b)$ with $(u,v)$, we obtain point
L342:  | $$\left(-y,\frac{-y\left(u^{2}+v^{2}\right)+uvx+y^{3}}{uv-xy}\right).$$  |
L343: 
L344: This point coincides with $Q_{3}$ for all $x$, which implies
L345: 
L346:  | $$ab=uv,\ a^{2}+b^{2}=u^{2}+v^{2}.$$  |
L347: 
L348: Hence either $u=b,v=a$, a butterfly, or $u=-b,v=-a$, an anti-butterfly, or $u=-a,v=-b$, symmetric opposite vertices.
L349: 
L350: It remains to consider the case when both pairs of opposite vertices of ${\mathbf{P}}$ are collinear. Then one may assume that
L351:  | $$P_{1}=(1,0),\ P_{2}=(0,1),\ P_{3}=(a,0),\ P_{4}=(0,b),\ Q_{1}=(x,y).$$  |
L352: 
L353: Using equation (cite64†9 ) consecutively, one calculates
L354: 
L355:  | $$Q_{5}=\left(\frac{x(a^{2}-y^{2})(b^{2}-y^{2})}{(a^{2}b^{2}-y^{2})(1-y^{2})},y\right).$$  |
L356: 
L357: Equating it to $Q_{1}$ yields
L358: 
L359:  | $$(a^{2}-y^{2})(b^{2}-y^{2})=(a^{2}b^{2}-y^{2})(1-y^{2}),$$  |
L360: 
L361: hence $(a^{2}-1)(b^{2}-1)=0.$ If $a=1$ or $b=1$, then $P_{1}=P_{3}$ or $P_{2}=P_{4}$, and if $a=-1$ or $b=-1$, we have the already considered symmetric case. ∎
L362: ### 2.5 Constructing $c$-related polygons
L363: 
L364: In this section we describe a construction that yields a pair of $c$-related $n$-gons. This is a centroaffine analog of a construction that yields pairs of polygons in the discrete bicycle correspondence that is described in [cite31†13 ].
L365: Assume first that $n$ is odd. Start with an $n$-gon (pentagon ${\mathbf{A}}$ in Figure cite65†6 ). Connect the midpoints of its sides with the origin. Consider the affine reflections in these lines that interchange the vertices of the respective sides of ${\mathbf{A}}$. Let $R$ be the composition of these reflections taken around the polygon.
L366: 
L367: Figure 6: Constructing a $c$-related pair of $n$-gons, odd $n$.
L368: ###### Lemma 2.8.
L369: 
L370: The map $R$ is an affine reflection.
L371: ###### Proof.
L372: 
L373: Since $n$ is odd, $R$ is orientation reversing and its determinant equals $-1$. Hence it has two eigendirections. Also $R$ has a fixed point, a vertex of ${\mathbf{A}}$. Therefore the eigenvalues of $R$ are $1$ and $-1$, and it is an affine reflection. ∎
L374: 
L375: It follows that $R^{2}=Id$. The construction of a $c$-related pair follows.
L376: 
L377: Start with an arbitrary point $P_{1}$ and apply consecutive affine reflections around the polygon ${\mathbf{A}}$ twice. This produces $2n$ points
L378:  | $$P_{1}\mapsto Q_{2}\mapsto P_{3}\mapsto Q_{4}\mapsto\cdots\mapsto Q_{n},$$  |
L379: 
L380: see cite65†6 . Each quadrilateral $P_{i}P_{i+1}Q_{i}Q_{i+1}$ is a centroaffine butterfly, therefore ${\bf P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\sim}}{\bf Q}$.
L381: 
L382: One has $c=[P_{1},Q_{1}]=[P_{1},R(P_{1})]$. The locus of points $P_{1}$ for which $[P_{1},R(P_{1})]$ is fixed is a hyperbola (indeed, $R$ is conjugated to the map $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)$, in which case this claim is obvious).
L383: Now consider the case of even $n$. We repeat the above construction, but this time the transformation $R$ had determinant 1. It still has an eigendirection with eigenvalue 1 (a vertex of ${\bf A}$ is a fixed point), but it is not necessarily the identity. We need to assume that $R=Id$, see below.
L384: 
L385: Figure 7: Constructing a $c$-related pair of $n$-gons, even $n$.
L386: With this assumption, we choose two starting points, $P_{1}$ and $Q_{1}$ and apply consecutive affine reflections to obtain polygons ${\bf P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\sim}}{\bf Q}$ with $c=[P_{1},Q_{1}]$ as before, see Figure cite66†7 .
L387: 
L388: We describe when the transformation $R$ is the identity. Recall that we consider the case of an even-gon.
L389: ###### Lemma 2.9.
L390: 
L391: One has $R=Id$ if and only if
L392: 
L393:  | $$\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{i}\frac{v_{2i}}{s_{2i-1}s_{2i+1}}=0.$$  |
L394: ###### Proof.
L395: 
L396: Since $R$ has a fixed point, a vertex of polygon ${\bf A}$, the transformation $R$ is the identity if and only if it has another fixed point not collinear with the first one. Thus we need to learn when a polygon ${\bf B}$ exists, not homothetic to ${\bf A}$, whose sides are parallel to those of ${\bf A}$ and the midpoints of whose sides are collinear to those of ${\bf A}$.
